learning_objective: 🎯 Play the detective! Learn how to find the missing clues when your Cash Book balance doesn't match the Bank Passbook balance.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: You maintain a Cash Book (Bank column). The bank maintains your account and gives you a Passbook. Ideally, the balances should be identical. But due to timing differences or errors, they rarely match on a given day.

Example: You write a cheque and deduct it from your Cash Book today. But the person deposits it in the bank 3 days later. For those 3 days, your Cash Book balance will be lower than the Passbook balance.
Sometimes the bank acts without telling you immediately. They might deduct bank charges or add interest directly to your Passbook. You only find out later, causing a mismatch.
A BRS is just a statement (not an account). You start with one balance (e.g., Cash Book), add or subtract the differences, and 'arrive' at the other balance (Passbook).

fun_activity.title: ⚖️ The Human Weighing Scale
fun_activity.instructions: Hold your left hand out (Cash Book) and right hand out (Passbook). If the Bank charges ₹100, the Passbook drops. To make the Cash Book equal the Passbook (if starting from Cash Book), you must DROP (subtract) the Cash Book hand!

exam_tips: 📌 Debit balance in Cash Book = Favourable (+). Credit balance in Cash Book = Overdraft (-).
📌 Credit balance in Passbook = Favourable (+). Debit balance in Passbook = Overdraft (-).
📌 Always identify your 'Starting Point' (e.g., Balance as per Cash Book). You can only adjust the book you started with to match the other book.
quick_recap: ⭐ BRS is a statement prepared to reconcile the difference between the Cash Book and Passbook balances.
⭐ Differences arise due to timing (unpresented/uncleared cheques) and direct bank actions (interest/charges).
⭐ Preparing an 'Amended Cash Book' first can simplify the BRS process.
